source_reviews.independent_solution: Let u and v be functions on the same interval, differentiable at a common point x, and let w=u-v. For every sufficiently small nonzero increment t allowed by that interval, (w(x+t)-w(x))/t=(u(x+t)-u(x))/t-(v(x+t)-v(x))/t. The first quotient tends to u'(x) and the second to v'(x), both finite by the differentiability assumption. The difference of these limits therefore exists and equals u'(x)-v'(x). By the definition of derivative, w'(x)=u'(x)-v'(x). Since x was arbitrary among common differentiability points, (u-v)'=u'-v' throughout that set. This proves the source assertion directly without assuming the subtraction rule being proved. Consistently with the selected sum theorem, the quotient for -v is the negative of v's quotient, so (-v)'=-v' and u-v=u+(-v) yields the same result.
